reporting-org.narrative: Obodo Centre for Advocacy and Equal Rights

description.narrative: 500 individuals have seen art from LGBTQI+ creators

Under the "Obodo International Artist Residency" we invited Black diaspora artists to collaborate with Nigerian artists, focusing on the intersection of arts and human rights. We called for artists interested in exploring how the former can be leveraged in dealing with societal norms and prejudices while advocating for LGBTQ+ people in Nigeria and beyond. The open call attracted a diverse range of artists (38 in total) who are passionate about using their art to promote parity and challenge existing societal norms. Out of the 38 applications we selected 3 artists to look at the role art plays in challenging narratives surrounding gender and sexual minorities while exploring the therapeutic potential of art. The selected projects focus on the importance of community as a means of providing safe spaces for LGBTQ+ people in Nigeria and include elements that contribute to long-term community support and resource sharing. To date, our first resident a multidisciplinary artist, filmmaker and Dj has completed her residency in Lagos. During her stay she hosted 2 events in the HRC with a total of 65 attendees. 20 guests and 5 performers at an intimate Womxn centric open mic night and 45 attendees at the film screening and exhibition. will also collaborate with local artists, engage in workshops, conversations, and have an exhibition of their work towards the end of their residency. "The artist residency program is off to a promising start with the selection of our first artist-in-residence, whom we have begun to engage with regarding their creative practice and community engagement activities, and is set to commence in September. Building on this momentum, we prepared a comprehensive open call for subsequent artists-in-residence, inviting individuals to propose community-centric and human rights-focused projects. The final two artists have been selected from this pool of applicants and are currently being onboarded.
To commemorate the launch of the Human Rights Centre, we hosted a public art exhibition featuring the works of seven queer artists, each bringing a unique perspective on themes of identity, resilience, and social justice through mediums of fashion, photography, multimedia among others. The exhibition was well-received, attracting an audience of 110 people on its opening night, and 102 additional persons on subsequent days. The exhibition drew a diverse crowd which included members of the LGBTQ+ and art community, allies, civil society organisations, foreign mission representatives, and art enthusiasts.
